transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky says his country's naval forces were responsible
for yesterday's attack on a Russian military ship off the coast of Libya.
In a post on social media, Zelensky says seven drones were involved in the strike.
Ukraine's attack on the Russian ship came days after Russia fired three cruise missiles
into Polish territory during military training exercises being conducted 30 to 60 miles away.
In eastern Iowa, the U.S. Army says it will carry out the controlled detonation of five
tons of unstable explosives containing lead on Wednesday.
As Eliza Billingham with Iowa Public Radio reports, a court order had put that detonation
on hold.
The Army says the lead azide has become unstable and must be disposed of.
An earlier planned controlled detonation had been delayed at the last minute after public
outcry and a lawsuit from environmental groups.
Michael Schmidt from the Iowa Environmental Council said federal officials didn't give
local leaders enough time to notify residents of the potential of lead-laden dust across
the region.
That would have allowed them to make informed decisions to protect the health and safety
of our communities.
But the Army said federal rules allow the Army to continue if there's imminent danger
to the public.
It says cold weather puts the already unstable chemical at too high a risk of uncontrolled
explosions so it will do the controlled detonation right before the holiday.
For NPR News, I'm Eliza Billingham in Iowa City.
UN climate talks have wrapped up in Turkey without an agreement to curb emissions.
NPR's Julia Simon reports.
It's the longest climate conference in history, yet the conference ended without a deal.
The conference works by consensus, and countries disagreed about whether or not the text should
mention transitioning away from fossil fuels.
Burning fossil fuels drives about 73 percent of planet heating emissions, yet some countries
like Saudi Arabia opposed fossil fuel language.
Frustrated with the United Nations Conference, more than 50 countries have started their
own conference.
It's focused on transitioning away from oil, gas, and coal, and will have its second convening
in July.
Meanwhile, countries are already moving away from oil and gas to solar and electric vehicles.
Not always for climate reasons, but economic ones.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
Triple A says gasoline and diesel prices in the U.S. continue their steady declines as
people travel this week for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Regular now averages about $3.64 a gallon.
That price has dropped about 65 cents in the last month.
Wall Street futures are sharply higher this morning following Friday's steep losses.
The NASDAQ lost more than 5 percent.
Dow futures are up more than one and three-quarters percent.
S&P futures are up more than two and a half percent.
This is NPR News.
Delta Airline says it has resolved a problem with one of its automated systems that delayed
more than a thousand flights yesterday in and out of Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International
Airport.
This issue also led to several dozen flights being canceled.
Delta says the system that calculates weight distribution for flights involving passengers,
baggage and fuel was not working.
The airline says some of the delays and cancellations stemmed from other issues, including weather
in the Northeastern U.S., where it was rainy.
In New York, a local wardrobe workers union has voted to authorize a strike as Broadway
shifts into the lucrative holiday season.
The move come weeks after union stagehands voted to do the same.
As Jeff London reports, the unions have been without a contract for months.
Both locals, which are members of the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees, or
IOTC, have been working without contracts since July.
The locals have been negotiating with the Broadway League, which represents theater
owners and producers, but no agreements have been reached.
A strike authorization is not the same as a strike, but with Broadway still in recovery
mode following an 18-month closure during the pandemic, a work stoppage around the period
from Thanksgiving to New Year's could cause great economic damage and a disruption for
audiences, many of whom travel to New York to see Broadway shows.
For NPR News, I'm Jeff London in New York.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Ukraine's Zelensky says Ukrainian naval forces struck a Russian military ship off Libya with drones
Iowa Army plans controlled detonation of five tons of unstable lead azide explosives near Iowa City
UN climate talks in Turkey end without agreement on curbing emissions or fossil fuel language
AAA reports US gasoline and diesel prices continuing steady declines ahead of Thanksgiving travel
Wall Street futures jump sharply after Friday's steep losses, with NASDAQ down over 5 percent
Delta resolves automated weight-distribution system glitch that delayed over a thousand Atlanta flights
New York wardrobe workers union authorizes strike as Broadway enters holiday season without contract
